JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, TECHNICAL MEMBER
1. Appeal No. 307 of 2017 has been filed by M/s Samalpatti Power
Corporation Pvt. Ltd. ("SPCL”) and an Appeal, No. 344 of 2017 has been filed
by Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution Corporation Limited ("TANGEDCO"),
against the Common Order dated 31.01.2017 passed by the Tamil Nadu
Electricity Regulatory Commission ("State Commission"/"TNERC") in M.A.P.
No. 2 of 2007 and M.A.P. No. 1 of 2012. The impugned Order determines the
admissible capital cost of the 105.66 MW diesel-based generating station of
SPCL and the consequential tariff parameters. SPCL is aggrieved by the
disallowance of certain components of the capital cost and the consequential tariff
determination made by the State Commission in Appeal No 307 of 2017, and
while TANGEDCO has challenged the findings relating to the debt-equity ratio
adopted for tariff determination in Appeal No 344 of 2017.
Page 3 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
Description of parties
2. The Appellant, in Appeal 307 of 2017, and Respondent No.1 in Appeal 344
of 2017, the M/s Samalpatti Power Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (hereinafter referred as
"SPCL") is a generating company engaged in the business of generation and
sale of electricity.
3. The Appellant in Appeal No 344 of 2017 and Respondent No.1 in Appeal
307 of 2017, the Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution Corporation Limited
(hereinafter referred as "TANGEDCO"), formerly known as the Tamil Nadu
Electricity Board ("TNEB"), is the distribution licensee in the State of Tamil Nadu.
Respondent No.2 in both the Appeals, the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory
Commission (hereinafter referred as “TNERC/ State Commission”) is the State
Electricity Regulatory Commission for the State of Tamil Nadu, discharging
statutory functions under the Electricity Act, 2003,
Brief facts are as under:
4. SPCL has proposed to establish a 100 MW diesel generating power station
(DGPP) at Bargur Industrial Complex, Krishnagiri District, Tamil Nadu for supply
of electricity to the erstwhile Tamil Nadu Electricity Board ("TNEB") and a
Memorandum of Understanding was executed on 18.02.1995.Subsequently, the
installed capacity of the project was enhanced from 100 MW to 105.66 MW, which
was approved by TNEB on 17.09.1997 and by the Government of Tamil Nadu on
21.09.1997. Approval under Section 44 of the then Electricity Supply Act 1948,
for setting up of 105.66 MW DGPP was accorded by TNEB.
Page 4 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
5. The Central Electricity Authority ("CEA") accorded Techno-Economic
Clearance ("TEC") to the project on 10.02.1998, prescribing, inter alia, the
approved project cost, debt-equity structure and other financial parameters.
Subsequently, a Power Purchase Agreement dated 22.05.1998 was executed
between SPCL and TNEB governing the sale and purchase of electricity from the
generating station. Thereafter, SPCL submitted the Firm Financial Package,
which was approved by the CEA on 12.08.1999 after financial appraisal of the
project. The project achieved financial closure on 24.12.1999.
6. The generating station achieved Commercial Operation on 01.03.2001.
Upon completion of the project, SPCL on 26.05.2001, submitted the completed
capital cost of Rs 424.827 Crore to CEA for approval. During scrutiny of the
completed capital cost, certain components of expenditure claimed by SPCL,
including financing charges, interest during construction, foreign exchange
variation, customs duty, liquidated damages, consultancy charges and other
allied expenses, became the subject matter of examination by the CEA.
7. Subsequent to the enactment of the Electricity Act, 2003, the jurisdiction
relating to determination of tariff vested with the State Commission. Since the
completed capital cost had not attained finality, TANGEDCO filed M.A.P. No.2 of
2007 before the State Commission seeking determination of the admissible
capital cost of the project. SPCL challenged the jurisdiction of the State
Commission before the Hon'ble Madras High Court by filing writ petitions.
However, the writ proceedings were ultimately withdrawn on 04.04.2012, and
SPCL itself filed M.A.P. No. 1 of 2012 before TNERC seeking approval of its
claimed completed capital cost. Since both the petitions related to determination
of capital cost of the same project, the State Commission heard them together.
Page 5 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
8. By the impugned order, the State Commission determined the completed
capital cost after allowing and disallowing various expenditure heads claimed by
SPCL. The State Commission in the Impugned Order approved the Capital cost
of subject project as Rs 419.05 Crore as against Rs 424.84 Crore claimed by
SPCL. The State Commission also determined the debt-equity ratio and other
tariff parameters for the project. While certain claims of the generating company
were accepted, several components of the capital expenditure were either
reduced or disallowed on the ground that they were not prudently incurred or
were unsupported by the material available on record.
9. TANGEDCO filed Appeal No. 344 of 2017 challenging the same common
order on a limited issue relating to the debt-equity ratio adopted by the State
Commission. According to TANGEDCO, the Commission failed to correctly apply
Regulation 21 of the TNERC Tariff Regulations, 2005, which mandates that where
actual equity employed is less than 30%, the actual debt and equity should alone
be considered. It is the specific case of TANGEDCO that, after determining the
completed capital cost, the Commission ought to have deducted the actual loan
availed by the generating company and treated only the balance as equity instead
of mechanically adopting a normative debt-equity ratio.
10. SPCL opposes the appeal filed by TANGEDCO and supports the findings
of the State Commission on the issue of debt-equity ratio, while simultaneously
assailing those findings of the Commission which resulted in reduction of the
admissible capital cost. Conversely, TANGEDCO supports the findings of the
Commission relating to disallowance of various capital expenditure but seeks
modification of the impugned order to the extent it adopts an incorrect debt-equity
ratio for tariff determination.
Page 6 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
11. We have heard Mr. Girik Bhalla, Mr. Vishrov Mukherjee, learned counsels
appearing on behalf of SPCL and Ms. Anusha Nagarajan, learned counsel
appearing on behalf of TANGEDCO at considerable length. We have also
considered the written submissions/note of arguments, the impugned Order, the
material on record. Since both the Appeals arise out of the common impugned
Order and involve interconnected issues relating to determination of the capital
cost and consequential tariff of the generating station, they are being disposed of
by this common judgement.
Issues in Appeal 307 of 2017 : SPCL has challenged disallowance of cost on
following accounts
1. Establishment and Construction Supervision Expenses
2. O&M Mobilization Fee
3. Development Expenses
4. Financial Advisory Fee
5. Legal and Stamping Fee
6. Management fee under Equity Raising Charges
7. Disallowance in soft Cost Due to reduction in hard Cost
8. Land Deposit paid to TACID
9. Construction Insurance
10. Interest During Construction
Learned Counsel on behalf of SPCL, has submitted that SPCL has given up its
claim on Issue No. 8 (i.e Land Deposit paid to TACID) and Issue No 9
Page 7 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
(Construction Insurances ) and Issue No 10 ( and Interest during Construction).
Accordingly these issues (No. 8,9,10) are disposed of as being not pressed.
Issues in Appeal 344 of 2017 :
TANGEDCO has challenged the Debt equity considered in the approved Capital
cost based on Normative ratio of 70:30, instead of considering entire debt taken
by SPCL and then working out the Debt : Equity Ratio for the approved capital
cost of the project.
Submissions urged on behalf of TANGEDCO in Appeal No. 344 of 2017
12. It is submitted that the Regulation 21 of the TNERC Tariff Regulations, 2005
clearly provides that while the amount of equity is limited to 30% of the capital
cost, there is no cap on the debt that may be availed for the project. In fact, where
the equity employed for the project is less than 30%, the actual debt amount has
to be considered. In the present case, SPCL admittedly drew a debt of Rs. 304.05
Crores, which was also approved by the TNERC. Accordingly, the TNERC ought
to have considered the approved capital cost of Rs 419.05 crores and deducted
the actual debt drawn from the said amount, resulting in an equity component of
Rs 115 Crore, constituting 27.44% of the project cost and a corresponding debt-
equity ratio of 72.56:27.44. Adopting a higher equity than what is permissible
under Regulation 21 would result in a greater tariff burden on the consumers.
13. Further, while fixing the debt-equity ratio in the Impugned Order on the basis
of equity infused in the project, the TNERC failed to consider any of the
submissions advanced by TANGEDCO on the issue. TNERC accepted SPCL's
claim that it had infused equity of Rs 129.36 Crore, despite the fact that such
Page 8 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
equity was computed on the basis of the capital cost of Rs 424.84 Crores claimed
by SPCL in its petition, while after undertaking a prudence check, the TNERC
approved a lower capital cost of Rs 419.05 Crore, consequently, there was no
legal or factual basis to adopt the equity figure of Rs 129.36 Crore which was
predicated upon the higher capital cost claimed by SPCL.
14. It is further submitted that SPCL for the first time in the present Appeal,
averred that the Tariff Regulations, 2005 are not applicable to the present case
and that the Tariff Regulations, 2002 are the applicable regulations. The
contention of SPCL that the Tariff Regulations, 2002 do not envisage any debt-
equity ratio and, therefore, the debt-equity ratio of 69.55:30.45 can be adopted,
as the PPA permits minor deviation in the debt-equity ratio, is wholly untenable,
as it has been raised for the first time at the stage of final arguments without any
supporting pleadings and, therefore, cannot be entertained. Further, the Tariff
Regulations, 2005 expressly provide that they came into force from the date of
their publication, i.e., 03.08.2005 [Regulation 1(3)], and are applicable for
determination of tariff under Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 [Regulation
1(5)]. Since TANGEDCO's tariff petition and SPCL's petition for determination of
capital cost were filed in 2007 and 2012 respectively, both petitions were clearly
governed by the Tariff Regulations, 2005. SPCL has also failed to establish any
basis for the applicability of the Tariff Regulations, 2002. Admittedly, its generating
station was commissioned on 01.03.2001, and if, on that basis, the 2005
Regulations are sought to be excluded, the 2002 Regulations would equally be
inapplicable. Moreover, SPCL did not challenge the finding of the TNERC fixing
the debt-equity ratio at 70:30 in Appeal No. 307 of 2017 in the Impugned Order
and has, therefore, accepted the said finding. It cannot now, in TANGEDCO's
Appeal, be permitted to assail the same at the stage of final arguments, nearly
ten years after the Impugned Order was passed. In any event, it is well settled
Page 9 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
that the regulations framed by the Electricity Commissions have an overriding
effect over contractual stipulations between the parties, as held by the Supreme
Court in “PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, (2010)
4 SCC 603. Accordingly, even if the PPA contemplated minor deviations in the
debt-equity ratio, upon the coming into force of the Tariff Regulations, 2005, the
determination of the debt-equity ratio is governed by the Regulations and not by
the contractual terms of the PPA.
Submission urged on behalf of the TANGEDCO in Appeal No. 307 of 2017
15. The Appellant’s contention that TNERC ought not to have looked at the TEC
and the FFP cost approved by the CEA for determination of the capital cost of the
Appellant's plant, and that the TNERC ought to have independently carried out a
prudence check to determine whether the capital cost claimed by the Appellant
was actually incurred is baseless. At the outset, it is submitted that this contention
has been raised by the Appellant for the first time at the stage of final arguments
in 2026, despite the Appeal having been filed in 2017. Further, several grounds
urged in the Appeal are themselves premised on the allegation that the TNERC
failed to consider the elements of the capital cost approved by the CEA under the
TEC and the FFP, including the grounds relating to disallowance of soft cost,
management fee, and establishment expenses.
16. It is further submitted that in its Petition for fixation of capital cost before the
TNERC (MAP No. 1 of 2012), the SPCL itself unequivocally relied upon the TEC
and the FFP approved by CEA. SPCL, itself has emphasized that the capital cost
for which approval was sought was lower than the approved FFP after adjustment
for foreign exchange, and relied upon the capital cost approved under the TEC
and revised in terms of the FFP, and placed point-wise reliance on various
Page 10 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
components of capital cost approved by the CEA under the TEC and/or the FFP,
such as Establishment & Development Expenditure, Operator Training and O&M
Mobilisation Fee. Having thus, founded its case before the Commission on the
TEC and the FFP, the Appellant cannot now be permitted to approbate and
reprobate by contending that the TNERC erred in relying upon the very same
approvals for determination of the capital cost. Such a contradictory stand is
legally impermissible. Moreover, acceptance of the Appellant's contention that the
TEC and the FFP ought to have been disregarded would lead to the absurd
consequence that the Appellant's generating station had no valid statutory
approval or clearance to operate.
17. It is further submitted that TEC and the FFP were approved by the CEA on
10.02.1998 and 12.08.1999 respectively under Section 43A of the Electricity
(Supply) Act, 1948 (subsequently omitted by the amendments of 2000), which
provided that determination of tariff would be in accordance with the norms and
guidelines laid down by the CEA. Accordingly, the grant of the TEC and the FFP,
as well as the determination of the capital cost of the Appellant's generating
station, were undertaken in accordance with the statutory scheme prevailing prior
to the enactment of the Electricity Act, 2003. Section 185(2)(a) of the Electricity
Act, 2003 expressly provides that anything done or any action taken under the
repealed Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 or any notification issued thereunder shall
be deemed to have been done or taken under the corresponding provisions of
the Electricity Act, 2003. This principle equally extends to tariff determinations
undertaken under the repealed statute, as held by this Tribunal in DVC v. JSERC
& Ors., Appeal No. 85 of 2009, dated 22.07.2009.
18. The aforesaid position is further reinforced by Section 6 of the General
Clauses Act, 1897, which provides that, unless a different intention appears, the
Page 11 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
repeal of a statute does not affect any right, privilege, obligation or liability
acquired or incurred thereunder. As held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State
of Punjab v. Mohar Singh, (1954) 2 SCC 483 the line of enquiry is not whether
the new enactment expressly keeps alive the rights and liabilities arising under
the repealed statute, but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. Thus,
the determination of the capital cost by the TNERC after considering the TEC and
the FFP approvals accorded by the CEA constitutes a valid determination. The
case law relied upon by SPCL to contend that the CEA no longer has any role in
approval of tariff after the commencement of the Electricity Act, 2003 has no
application to the present case, since no approval of tariff is being sought from
the CEA. None of the judgments relied upon by SPCL hold that the statutory
clearances and approvals granted by the CEA prior to the coming into force of
the Electricity Act, 2003 become nugatory or invalid.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF SPCL
19. It is submitted that, upon the enactment of the Electricity Regulatory
Commissions Act, 1998 and the Notifications dated 22.03.1999 and 11.09.2000
issued thereunder, the erstwhile regime of tariff determination based on the
norms prescribed by the Central Electricity Authority stood discontinued and the
statutory power to determine tariff vested exclusively in the respective State
Electricity Regulatory Commissions.
20. It is further submitted that, in exercise of its statutory powers, the TNERC
notified the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission Tariff Regulations,
2002 on 21.08.2002 under Section 58 of the Electricity Regulatory Commissions
Act. The said Regulations prescribed the tariff fixation framework applicable to
power projects within the State of Tamil Nadu. Particular reliance was placed on
Page 12 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
Regulation 6, which, inter alia, mandates that tariff should be rationalised on the
basis of the actual cost of generation, transmission and distribution of electricity
and should provide a level playing field for all utilities so as to promote private
sector participation in the electricity sector. Subsequently, with the coming into
force of the Electricity Act, 2003, Section 86 vested the State Commission with
the exclusive jurisdiction to determine tariff, which continued under the TNERC
Tariff Regulations, 2005 notified in supersession of the Tariff Regulations, 2002.
It was submitted that the determination of the completed capital cost of SPCL's
Project in M.A.P. No. 1 of 2012 and M.A.P. No. 2 of 2007 was required to be
undertaken in accordance with the aforesaid statutory and regulatory framework.
21. Regulation 6(3) of the Tariff Regulations, 2002 read with the definition of
"Capital Cost" under the Power Purchase Agreement dated 22.05.1998 requires
the completed capital cost and tariff to be determined on the basis of the actual
expenditure incurred by the Appellant in establishing the Project.
22. It is submitted that the Commission is bound by its own Tariff Regulations
and cannot adopt a methodology contrary thereto, as held by the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in PTC India Ltd. v. CERC, (2010) 4 SCC 603. Further this
Tribunal in its judgment in “NTPC v. CERC” (Appeal Nos. 151 and 152 of 2007),
held that the entire value of capital asset, as soon as the same is put into
operation is recoverable by way of capital cost.
23. Present case pertains to tariff determination under Section 62 of the
Electricity Act, which is based on the cost-plus regime. Under such regime,
prudent capital and operational expenditure are allowable as pass-through in
tariff, subject only to prudence check by the State Commission. Reliance was
also placed on the Judgment of this Tribunal in Damodar Valley Corporation v.
Page 13 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
CERC & Ors. (Appeal No. 273 of 2007), wherein it was held that tariff is a
reflection of the actual cost of supply and, unless the expenditure incurred by the
generating company is found to be imprudent, the same is required to be allowed
as a pass-through in tariff.
24. It is submitted that “TNERC did not follow the statutory mandate of Section
86 when determining the capital cost”. Majority of the disallowances in the
Impugned Order are founded on the premise that wherever the actual
expenditure under any line item exceeded the cost approved by the CEA in the
TEC or the FFP, the admissible capital cost was required to be restricted to the
CEA-approved amount. It was contended that, by adopting such a rigid approach,
the Commission abdicated its statutory obligation of determining tariff in
accordance with the TNERC Tariff Regulations, 2002 and failed to undertake the
prudence check of the actual and legitimate expenditure incurred by the
Appellant, as mandated under the Electricity Act. It was further submitted that the
Commission confined its consideration only to public interest while ignoring the
other guiding principles contained in Section 61 of the Electricity Act. Learned
Counsel further submitted that, upon the repeal of the Electricity (Supply) Act,
1948 with the coming into force of the Electricity Act, 2003, the requirement of
CEA approval for schemes or capital cost of generating stations ceased to have
any statutory basis. It was contended that the functions of the CEA under the
Electricity Act are confined to those enumerated under Section 73 and do not
extend to approval of capital expenditure or determination of completed capital
cost, as recognised by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in U.P. Power Corporation
Ltd. v. NTPC Ltd. and by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in GVK Industries Ltd.
v. CEA, which held that the CEA performs only an advisory role, whereas the
statutory duty and exclusive jurisdiction to determine tariff and capital cost vest
with the State Commission.
Page 14 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
25. It is further submitted that “Impugned order is violative of Electricity act,
Tariff Regulations, 2002 and Tariff Regulations, 2005”. SPCL claimed a completed
capital cost of Rs 424.84 Crores in M.A.P. No. 1 of 2012, duly verified and certified
by its Statutory Auditors, which constitutes the actual expenditure incurred and
forms part of the capital cost in terms of Regulation 6(3) of the TNERC Tariff
Regulations, 2002 and Regulations 18(2) and 18(3) of the Tariff Regulations,
2005. While the TEC dated 10.02.1998 approved a tentative capital cost of Rs
391.86 Crore, subject to the FFP, the FFP dated 12.08.1999 approved a tentative
capital cost of Rs. 390.82 Crore, which was expressly subject to variation on
account of exchange rate fluctuations and Change in Law. On adjustment for the
exchange rate prevailing on the Commercial Operation Date, the CEA-approved
capital cost under the FFP worked out to Rs 431.38 Crores. Despite the aforesaid
position, the Commission allowed only Rs 419.05 Crores as the completed capital
cost, thereby disallowing Rs 5.79 Crore from the actual expenditure incurred by
SPCL, even though the capital cost so allowed remained Rs12.33 Crores lower
than the CEA-approved capital cost under the adjusted FFP. It was contended
that the Commission has neither disputed that the said expenditure was actually
incurred for construction of the Project nor recorded any finding that such
expenditure was imprudent.
26. Prudence check of the capital cost is required to be undertaken strictly in
accordance with Regulation 18 of the TNERC Tariff Regulations, 2005, as the
Electricity Act does not define the scope of "prudence check". Reliance was
placed on the judgments of this Tribunal in Dodson-Lindblom Hydro Power Pvt.
Ltd. v. MERC (Appeal No. 152 of 2010) and PGCIL v. CERC (Appeal No. 99 of
2013), wherein it has been held that prudence check must be carried out in
accordance with the applicable Tariff Regulations and the benchmark norms
prescribed by the Regulatory Commission.
Page 15 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
27. Learned Counsel submits that the capital cost claimed by SPCL was well
within the capital cost claimed and allowed by the Commission in respect of
similarly placed projects, particularly MPC Project. It was submitted that, although
the TEC granted to MPC was lower than that of SPCL, SPCL's Project
additionally included construction of a township comprising a housing colony and
an external water supply system, which did not form part of MPC's scope. Despite
this additional scope of work, MPC claimed a completed capital cost of Rs 429.01
Crores as against SPCL's claim of Rs 424.84 Crore, and the Commission
ultimately allowed a completed capital cost for MPC which was approximately Rs
8.70 Crores higher than that allowed to SPCL, notwithstanding that both projects
were of identical capacity, had the same contracted quantum, and were
constructed and commissioned during the same period. Therefore, it is
contended that the Commission ought to have adopted the same parameters
while determining the completed capital cost of SPCL's Project.
28. Reliance was also placed on the recent Judgment of this Tribunal dated
04.09.2025 in Delhi Transco Ltd. v. CERC & Ors. (Appeal No. 223 of 2022),
wherein it was held that normative rates serve only as benchmarks and cannot
override the requirement of determining tariff based on actual cost where reliable
data is available, as application of normative rates resulting in denial of actual
expenditure would be contrary to the principles of cost-reflective tariff and
financial viability.
OUR CONSIDERATION ; APPEAL NO 344 of 2017
29. The dispute in the present Appeal is confined to one issue, namely,
whether, in determining, the approved capital cost of the project, the entire debt
availed by SPCL is to be considered first and the balance treated as equity, or
Page 16 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
whether debt and equity are to be reckoned in the normative ratio of 70:30, such
that equity deployed does not exceed 30% of the capital cost. Learned Counsel
for TANGEDCO, placing reliance on Regulation 21 of the TNERC Tariff
Regulations, 2005, submitted that while equity is capped at 30% of the capital
cost, there is no restriction on the quantum of debt that may be availed for the
project. In the present case, SPCL admittedly availed debt of Rs. 304.05 Crore.
Therefore, in the approved capital cost of Rs 419.05 Crore, the entire debt of Rs
304.05 Crore ought to have been considered, with the balance Rs. 115 Crore
treated as equity, resulting in a debt–equity ratio of 72.56:27.44.
30. Per contra, learned Counsel for SPCL contended that the Tariff Regulations,
2002 and not Tariff Regulations 2005, are applicable to the present case, which
do not prescribe any debt–equity ratio. It was urged that a ratio of 69.55:30.45
may be adopted, as the PPA permits minor deviation in the debt–equity ratio. This
contention was opposed by TANGEDCO on the ground that it was raised for the
first time at the stage of final arguments without any supporting pleadings, and
therefore cannot be entertained.
31. We find no merit in the contention of SPCL that equity higher than 30%
should be considered merely because the PPA permits minor deviation. In its own
cross-appeal (Appeal No. 307 of 2017), SPCL accepted the debt–equity ratio of
70:30 and did not raise any issue on this aspect. It is, therefore, not open to SPCL
to raise such contention now, particularly in the appeal filed by TANGEDCO
contesting the debt : equity ratio allowed by the commission.
32. Further, we find it unnecessary to deliberate upon the applicability of the
2002 Tariff Regulations versus 2005 Tariff Regulations as contended by SPCL
now, as SPCL themselves have relied upon both the Tariff Regulations in their
Page 17 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
appeal and accepted the normative 70:30 debt : equity ratio as approved in the
Impugned Order. The Tribunal is therefore only required to clarify the meaning or
treatment of debt–equity ratio in the approved capital cost.
33. It is a settled principle that Regulatory Commissions, in discharge of their
statutory mandate, prescribe a normative debt–equity ratio, most commonly
70:30, for tariff determination. This prescription is intended to secure uniformity in
treatment across generating stations, to insulate tariff fixation from the vagaries
of individual financing structures, and to safeguard consumer interest by ensuring
that tariff is not unduly burdened by a typical capital structuring.
34. TANGEDCO has placed reliance upon the judgment of the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in “PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission”; (2010) 4 SCC 603 to contend that the Regulations framed by the
Regulatory Commission have overriding effect over the existing or future
contractual stipulations contained in the PPA. The ratio of the said judgment
makes it clear that the Regulations framed in exercise of the statutory power of
the Regulatory Commission govern the determination of tariff and cannot be
displaced by a contractual stipulation contained in the PPA. While we have
already deliberated the issue of minor variation in the Debt : Equity ratio in the
PPA, the issue in the present appeal pertains to interpretation of Debt : equity
ratio to be considered for a project.
35. We are of the considered view that once a component of capital expenditure
claimed by the petitioner is found inadmissible upon prudence check and is
consequently excluded from the approved capital cost, the normative debt–equity
ratio must be applied to the capital cost as finally admitted by the Commission,

overall execution and commissioning of the power plant of this magnitude and it
would have a cost also for performing various activities but at the same time, we
should not have an oversight of the overall expenditure required to be done which
would be capitalized on commercial operation declaration of the various units in
the power plant which would define the fixed cost. This Tribunal did not interfere
Page 35 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
with the disallowance made by State Commission under the head and observed
that since final cost is still to be worked out, State Commission while finalizing
the final completed cost would definitely look into all the elements of cost vis-à-
vis expenditure incurred by the Appellant since the inception of the project till
COD of the power plant.
74. The aforesaid judgement does not, by any stretch of imagination, seeks to
done away with the prudence check of the cost incurred even on account of
activities related to project management . Disallowance in the present issue is
on account of lack of documentary evidence and method of apportionment of
expenses to SPCL on the part of promoter companies, in the absence of which
prudence check cannot be carried out.
75. Accordingly, we find no error in the approach adopted by the State
Commission and no infirmity in the Impugned Order on this issue. The Impugned
Order is, therefore, upheld.
ISSUE NO 4 : FINANCIAL ADVISORY FEE
76. The FFP provides for Financial Advisory fee of 0.5 % of debt amount. An
amount of Rs. 25.2 lakhs has been disallowed under this head, considering 0.5
% of financial advisory fee on approved debt component of Rs. 295.47 Crore.
Relevant paragraph of Impugned Order is extracted as under :
“13.32.7. Commission’s findings:
As per the FFP approved by the CEA, the Financial Advisory Fee has been
calculated at 0.5% of the Debt amount which resulted in Rs.1.379 Crores.
This amount is arrived on the total debt amount of Rs.275.891
Crores.(275.891 Cr. * 0.5% = 1.379Crores).
Page 36 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
In the CEA’s Record Notes on discussion dated 13th January 2005, in para
37, the Director (F & CA) has also stated that “IPP has indicated more amount
on certain items of financing charges. Chairman said that these charges
would be restricted as per the approved Financial Package or actual
whichever is less”.
Though the total debt sanctioned for the project is Rs.311.2 Crores and the
actual debt drawn for the project is Rs.304.05 Crores, Commission is
considering a Debt Equity ratio of 70: 30 on the final completed cost of the
Project and in the FFP also, the CEA has considered a Debt Equity ratio of
70: 30. In the FFP, the Financing Charges amounting to Rs.1.379 Crores has
been calculated considering Debt at 70% of the Project Cost.
Hence, Commission allows the financing charges on the Debt amount of
Rs.295.474 Crores and calculated the financing charges at 0.5% on this
amount which resulted in a disallowance of Rs.0.258 Crore (Rs.1.738 Cr. -
Rs.1.48 Cr.). If the total debt drawn amounting to Rs.304.05 Crores is
considered then the total amount of Rs.311.2 Crores sanctioned as loan
would also be considered. But here, as the loan is limited to 70% of the Project
cost even though Debt and Equity is available in excess than what is required
for this project. The amount already disputed by TANGEDCO is only Rs.0.252
Crore. Hence, the amount disputed by TANGEDCO under the head
amounting to Rs.0.252 Crore is disallowed.”
77. The Appellant has claimed Rs 1.738 Crore of Financial advisory fee on
account of multi lender structure of the project financing. It is evident from above
that in the FFP, total debt amount of Rs.275.891 Crore was considered and
accordingly the Financial advisor fee was worked out as Rs1.379 Crore (275.891
* 0.5% = 1.379 Crore).
78. Financial advisory services, in the context of project financing, are primarily
directed towards structuring debt, negotiating terms with lenders, and ensuring
bankability of the project. The advisor’s role is intrinsically tied to the quantum of
debt mobilized, since the complexity, risk assessment, and negotiation effort
scale with the size of borrowings. In the DPR of the subject project, the financial
advisory fee has been capped at 0.5 % of debt and same has been approved
under the FFP, though quantified based on then envisaged debt component in
Page 37 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
the project. The actual debt approved as part of allowed capital cost in the
Impugned Order is Rs. 295.47 Crore, however there is no dispute that debt
sanctioned for the project is Rs.311.2 Crore. We are of considered view that
Appellant is entitled to Financial advisory fee of 0.5 % on sanctioned debt amount
of Rs 311.2 Crore, instead of restricting it to approved debt component in the
approved capital cost.
79. To this limited extent, the Impugned Order warrants modification.
Accordingly, the Financial Advisory charges of 0.5 % on the sanctioned debt
amount of Rs 311.2 Crore is allowed.
ISSUE 5 : LEGAL AND STAMPING FEE
80. SPCL has claimed a Legal and Stamping Fee of approx. 42 lakhs, while the
same has been capped at the lumpsum value of Rs 37.5 Lakh as approved in the
FFP. The relevant portion of the Impugned Order is extracted hereunder:
“13.33.7. Commission’s findings:
The CEA vide letter No.2/TN/31/96-PAC/7005-27, dated 12th August 1999
has approved the FFP subject to certain conditions. The first such condition
is that “the project shall be executed in accordance with this approved
financial package and no change shall be made without prior approval of the
concerned State Government and Central Electricity Authority.”
While according approval for FFP, under the head Financing Charges, CEA
has considered only a lump sum amount of Rs.37.5 lakhs in respect of Legal
and Stamping Fees.
Record Notes of CEA
“Para37 Director (F & CA) stated that the IPP has indicated more amount on
certain items of financing charges. Chairman said that these charges would
be restricted to as per the approved financial package or actual whichever is
less.”
When there is a specific approval of expenditure to be incurred, the same
shall not exceed the approved quantum. Increase in expenses will
automatically increase the completed cost of the project. Comparison with
Page 38 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
other IPP’s should not be made where no FFP approval was accorded by
CEA to the other IPP. Hence, the Stamping and legal charges is allowed to
the extent of Rs.37.5 lakhs and an additional expenditure amounting to
Rs.4,50,000/- incurred over and above the FFP is disallowed.”
81. Learned counsel on behalf of SPCL submitted that Legal and stamping
fees in project finance are statutory and transactional costs incurred on the
execution of loan documentation. Stamp duty is a function of the value of loan
instruments executed, which is based on the sanctioned quantum of loans, which
in the present case is Rs. 311.2 Crore. It is further submitted that the lump sum
provision of Rs. 37.5 Lakhs in the FFP was computed on the basis of the then-
projected loan amount and exchange rate considering that the capital cost
envisaged in the FFP was Rs. 391 Crore. As the actual loan sanctioned was
higher (Rs. 311.2 Crore versus the FFP debt of Rs. 275.891 Crore), the additional
stamp duty and legal documentation charges were necessarily proportionally
higher. The State Commission ignored SPCL's demonstrated position that even
the "restated" legal & stamping fee (computed at the actual BFXR of Rs.
44.607/USD) comes to Rs. 41.4 Lakhs, a figure that corresponds almost exactly
to the actual expense of Rs. 41.9 Lakhs .
82. Legal and stamping fees are generally the costs incurred during the
execution of contracts, loan agreements, and other binding documents in a
project or financial transaction and these are treated as legitimate pre-operative
expenses. Considering that the amount of debt considered at the time of FFP
approval was lower as compared to the actual debt sanction amount of Rs. 311.2
Crore, it may result in higher Legal and stamping charges, which is the case in
present issue. Accordingly, we find merit in the submissions made by SPCL and
Impugned Order need interference. We further note that there seems to be no
dispute with regard to actual amount incurred by SPCL under this head, other
Page 39 of 46

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 307 of 2017 & 344 of 2017
than restricting it to Lump sum amount of Rs 37.5 lakh in terms of FFP approval.
We set aside the disallowance of Rs 4.5 lakh in the Impugned Order under the
subject issue.
ISSUE NO 6 : MANAGEMENT FEE UNDER EQUITY RAISING CHARGES
83. The Impugned Order has allowed Rs 47.6 lakhs as management fee under
equity raising charges and disallowed Rs. 12.4 Lakhs out of the Rs. 60 lakhs
claimed by SPCL (Management Fee Rs. 50 lakh + Other Fee Rs. 10 lakh).
Relevant paragraph of Impugned Order is extracted hereunder :
“13.34.5.Commission’s findings:
While according approval of FFP, under Equity Raising Charges, the
CEA has considered the Management fee only in respect of the Ogden
Energy II. Ogden Energy is the only investor under “Others” category.
CEA has approved 0.75% on the equity to be brought in by Ogden
Energy.
Hence, the excess expenditure amount of Rs.12.40 lakhs is hereby
disallowed.”
84. It is not in dispute that the Management Fee of 0.75% was provided on the

J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The appellant, a consumer in the State of Uttar Pradesh, has assailed
the order dated 27.01.2022 passed by the 1st respondent Uttar Pradesh
Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the
Commission”) whereby the Commission dismissed the review petition filed
by the appellant seeking review of tariff order dated 07.10.2008 vide which
the Commission had approved the capital cost of the power project of the
2nd respondent M/s Jaiprakash Power Ventures Limited and had determined
tariff for the same.
2. Facts of the case, briefly stated, are that the 2nd respondent developed
and commissioned a run of the river underground hydroelectric power project
with an installed capacity of 400MW (4x100MW) located across river
Alaknanda in district Chamoli in the State of Uttarakhand. A Power Purchase
Agreement (PPA) dated 16.01.2007 was executed between the 2nd
respondent and the 3rd respondent Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited
(UPPCL) for the sale of the entire power from the project, which was
approved by the Commission. Thereafter, the 2nd respondent filed petition
no.443/2007 seeking approval of capital cost to the tune of Rs.1682.72
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.195 of 2023 Page 3 of 11

crores as on the Commercial Operation Date (COD) of the project, which
was duly approved by the Commission vide order dated 05.04.2007 read
with order dated 12.04.2007.
3. Subsequently, the 2nd respondent filed Petition No.550/2008 seeking
approval of Rs.1715.58 crores as capital cost of the power project and
determination of tariff based on the same. The petition was disposed of by
the Commission vide order dated 07.10.2008 thereby granting reliefs as
sought by the 2nd respondent with further directions to the 3rd respondent
UPPCL to continue making payments to 2nd respondent based on PPA dated
16.01.2007 as well as relevant orders of the Commission.
4. In the year 2021, the appellant approached the Commission with
petition no.1702/2021 under Section 94(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 read
with Regulation 51 of Uttar Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2019 for review of the said order dated
07.10.2008 passed in petition no.550/2008. The review petition has been
rejected by the Commission vide impugned order dated 27.01.2022, which
has been assailed in the instant appeal.
5. We have heard Mr. Anand K. Ganesan, learned counsel for the
appellant, Mr. B.P. Patil, learned senior counsel appearing for the 2nd
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.195 of 2023 Page 4 of 11

respondent and Mr. Aditya K. Singh, learned counsel for the 3rd respondent.
We have also perused the written submissions filed by the learned counsels.
6. On being questioned as to how the instant appeal is maintainable as
having been filed against an order rejecting the review petition, the learned
counsel for the appellant argued that the appellant’s petition before the
Commission was, in substance, a petition for invocation of plenary statutory
powers of the Commission to determine tariff under Section 62(1)(a) and
86(1)(a) & (b) of the Electricity Act, 2003. It is his submission that the
appellant’s petition before the Commission was not actually a petition for
review of the tariff order dated 07.10.2008, and therefore, the Commission
has erred in applying the standards applicable to petitions filed under Order
XLVII Rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code. He would argue that revision of
tariff is distinct from review of tariff order and since the tariff determination is
a continuous process, the Commission is empowered to amend or alter the
tariff order whenever circumstances so warrant, either suo motu or upon an
application by any concerned person/entity. He submitted that the
Commission ought to have exercised its jurisdiction in public interest for
determination of correct tariff for the sale of power to the distribution licensee
i.e. the 3rd respondent.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.195 of 2023 Page 5 of 11

7. We do not feel convinced with these submissions made by the learned
counsel for the appellant as these are not only devoid of any merit but also
are not borne out from the record.
8. The petition filed by the appellant before the Commission was
captioned as: -
“IN THE MATTER OF:
Petition under Section 94(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003
read with Regulation 51 of the Uttar Pradesh Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business)
Regulations, 2019 for review of the order dated
07.10.2008 passed by the Hon’ble Commission in Petition
no.550/2008.”
(Emphasis supplied)
9. Section 94(1)(f) empowers a State Regulatory Commission to review
its decisions, directions, and orders. It is a power conferred upon the
Commission akin to power of review available to the civil courts under Order
XLVII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedures 1908. Therefore, manifestly
the appellant’s petition before the Commission was for review of the tariff
order dated 07.10.2008 and not for revision or alteration of the tariff. Further,
the prayers made in the petition are also important to note and are extracted
hereinbelow: -
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.195 of 2023 Page 6 of 11

“a) admit the present Review Petition after condoning the
delay, if any;
b) review the Impugned Order dated 07.10.2008 to the
extent that it violates this Commission's own regulations, as
enacted from time to time, by allowing JPVL to charge and
recover from UPPCL such rates for the sale of electricity
from the Project that are computed without the approval of
this Commission.
c) Initiate a fresh scrutiny and tariff determination exercise in
respect of JPVL by giving effect to the generation tariff
regulations of this Hon'ble Commission from 2009 onwards,
to examine whether the rates being charged since
01.04.2009 for sale of electricity by JPVL are in accordance
with the parameters prescribed by the generation tariff
regulations as enacted by this Commission, from time to
time;
d) In view of the prayer (c) above, direct JPVL to refund all
excess recoveries, that are not in consonance with the
parameters prescribed by the Regulations of this
Commission since 01.04.2009 till date, to UPPCL along with
18% interest.
e) Direct JPVL to file a fresh application for determination of
tariff in terms of the Commission's 2019 generation Tariff
Regulations for sale of power from its Project to UPPCL.”
(Emphasis supplied)
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.195 of 2023 Page 7 of 11

10. Prayer (a) and (b) clearly indicate that the petition was for review of the
order dated 07.10.2008. Prayers (c) and (d) are ancillary to the prayers (a)
and (b) and would have kicked in only in case the Commission made up its
mind to review the order dated 07.10.2008 by granting the prayers (a) and
(b). Therefore, the prayers made before the Commission were effectively
for review of the tariff order dated 07.10.2008.
11. Learned counsel for the appellant has failed to point out anything from
the record to show or suggest that the appellant had approached the
Commission for tariff revision and not for review of the tariff order dated
07.10.20008. In fact, the appellant had begun its submissions before the
Commission, as noted in the impugned order, by stating that the impugned
tariff order is erroneous on the face of record as the same was passed in
violation of 2004 Tariff Regulations which constitutes an error apparent on
the face of record. The grounds raised by the appellant in its petition before
the Commission have been noted in Paragraph nos.4 to 12 of the impugned
order. Paragraph nos.11 and 12 are material on the aspect under
consideration and are extracted hereinbelow: -
“Jurisdiction of this Commission
11. In terms of Section 94(1)(f) of the Act, this Commission
has the power to review its own orders/ decisions. Further,
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.195 of 2023 Page 8 of 11

in terms of Regulation 51(a) of the CBR, 2019, this Hon'ble
Commission has the requisite power to review its own
orders. The Regulation 51, in relevant part, has been
extracted below:
"51. Review of the decisions, directions, and orders: a.
Any person aggrieved by a direction, decision or order
of the Commission, from which (i) no appeal has been
preferred or (ii) from which no appeal is allowed, may
file a review, subject to provisions of Civil Procedure
Code, within ninety (90) days of the date of the
direction, decision or order, as the case may be to the
Commission."
12. The invocation of the power of review of this Hon'ble
Commission is not contingent upon the party who seeks
such invocation. In other words, there is no bar in respect of
who can approach this Hon'ble Commission seeking a
review of its own orders that have been envisaged in the
aforementioned provisions. This principle is clearly borne
out of the terms used in Regulation 51 itself, which states
that "Any person aggrieved by a direction, decision or order
of the Commission,..... may file a review." It is clear that this
could be any person who is aggrieved and is not limited, in
any manner, to such a person being a generating company,
a licensee, or being parties to the main dispute.”
(Emphasis supplied)
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.195 of 2023 Page 9 of 11

12. It is limpid from perusal of these two paragraphs of the impugned order
that the appellant had actually approached the Commission for seeking
review of the tariff order dated 07.10.2008 in terms of Section 94(1)(f) of the
Act read with Regulation 51(a) of UPERC(Conduct of Business) Regulations,
2019. It is nowhere the case of the appellant that the contents of these
Paragraphs of the impugned order are false and incorrect. Therefore, it does
not lie in the mouth of the appellant to contend before this Tribunal that the
petition filed by the appellant before the Commission was actually for revision
of tariff and not for review of the tariff order dated 07.10.2008.
13. We may also note that on the basis of the contentions raised in the
petition by the appellant, following two issues were framed by the
Commission for its consideration: -
“17. The Commission has framed the following issues for
deciding the admissibility / maintainability of the Review
Petition and has dealt in the succeeding paras below:
Issue I: Whether the Review Petition is barred by Limitation
Issue II: Whether there is any error apparent on the face of
the record i.e., the Commission's order dated
07.10.2008 in Petition No. 550 of 2008.”
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.195 of 2023 Page 10 of 11

14. The appellant has nowhere raised any grievance with regards to
formulation of these two issues by the Commission for its consideration.
15. Considering the tone and tenor of the averments made by the appellant
in its petition before the Commission and the submissions made on his behalf
during the hearing of the petition before the Commission, there does not
remain any iota of doubt with regards to the fact that petition filed by the
appellant was actually for review of the tariff order dated 07.10.2008 and not
for revision of tariff. As already noted hereinabove, the petition has been
rejected by the Commission vide impugned order dated 27.01.2022. Since
Rule 7 of Order XLVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 bars filing of
appeal against an order rejecting the review petition, the instant appeal is
clearly not maintainable and liable to be dismissed forthwith.
16. Accordingly, the appeal is hereby dismissed as being not maintainable.
All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of accordingly.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 02nd day of September, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Technical Mem ber (Electricity)
